newsitem.title: USA: Dollar up on mark as U.S. economy keeps growing.
newsitem.headline: Dollar up on mark as U.S. economy keeps growing.

text.p: The dollar rallied to a new three-year high against the German mark on Thursday on fresh signs that the U.S. economy is outpacing Germany's and on growing expectations of a U.S. interest rate hike.

The dollar rose for a ninth consecutive day, to 1.7210 marks in early U.S. trading after Germany reported that the number of jobless workers rose by 5,000, while the German unemployment rate was stuck at a stubbornly high 12.2 percent in February.
It got an extra boost from U.S. data showing claims for unemployment benefits dropped to 310,000 last week, from 316,000 the previous week, and a 2.5 percent jump in January factory orders.

"The point is, there is probably a very small likelihood that German rates are going to go up but ... U.S. rates will have a tendency to go up," said Diego Giurleo, a treasury vice president at Royal Bank of Canada in New York.
"Fundamentally speaking, you have growth on the dollar side and you have strong interest rate differentials," he added.

Odds that the Federal Reserve will raise interest rates at some point this year seemed to increase in recent days after Fed Chairman Alan Greenspan told Congress that tighter credit might be needed to prevent inflation from creeping up.

Traders said the dollar received some support after the head of Germany's powerful machine plant and construction industry organisation said on Thursday it would be appropriate for the dollar to strengthen to a range of 1.80 to 2.0 marks.

"It makes sense for them to lobby for a weaker mark. If you are going to take their jobs away and you are going to cut back on their benefits, they have to look for some way to stay competitive, to at least keep their jobs," said John Barlow, senior dealer at Bayerische Landesbank Girozentrale.
A weaker mark helps boost German exports by making the country's products less expensive overseas.

Thursday's rally soon ran out of steam as the market squared up before important U.S. employment data on Friday. The dollar eased against the Japanese yen after comments by U.S. Treasury Secretary Robert Rubin suggested trade frictions with Japan were percolating.
"There is some reluctance to get involved ahead of (the February U.S. employment data) tomorrow," said Alfonso Alejo, corporate foreign exchange manager at Sakura Bank Ltd.
"There was a little more forcefulness in (selling) the dollar against the yen, just because Rubin's comment has more bearing" on the market, he said.
The dollar ended at 1.7160 marks, up from 1.7127 late Wednesday. It fell to 121.08 yen from 121.15 yen.
On Thursday, Rubin told reporters in Washington that a sustained current account surplus by Japan was in "nobody's interest."

The Treasury chief's remark came on the heels of a report from Japan showing the surplus in its current account -- the broadest measure of a country's trade in goods and services -- surged in January from a year ago, its first increase in 17 months.

The dollar tends to fall when Japan's surplus swells, since traders fear the Clinton administration may try to reverse the dollar's recent rally on grounds that it has made U.S. exports too expensive and given Japan a trade advantage.
In other trading, the dollar edged up to 1.4820 Swiss francs from 1.4815 on Wednesday. It fell to Canadian $1.3647 from C$1.3692. The pound slipped to $1.6143 from $1.6155.
